citation: Bourne PE. Ten simple rules for making good oral presentations. PLoS Comput Biol. 2007;3(4):e77.
supports: Know the audience, rehearse with colleagues, leave room for questions. More than one visual per minute is called too many, as a personal rule of thumb.
limit: Opinion from experience. No data behind any rule.

citation: Naegle KM. Ten simple rules for effective presentation slides. PLoS Comput Biol. 2021;17(12):e1009554.
supports: One idea per slide, design for a distracted listener, keep backup slides, prepare for technical failure.
limit: The one-minute and six-element rules are advice, not tested claims.

citation: Alley M, content editor. Assertion-Evidence Approach: Rethinking Scientific and Technical Presentations. Leonhard Center, Penn State. Undated web resource.
supports: A complete-sentence headline supported by visual evidence, with secondary detail in the notes.
limit: Written by the method's advocate.

citation: Craft of Scientific Communication. Assertion-Evidence Tutorial. Undated web page.
supports: Steps for building a headline and evidence, then explaining the visual in your own sentences.
limit: Advocacy source. No numeric limits given.

citation: Assertion-Evidence Approach. Dissertation defense tutorial. Undated web page.
supports: Present a slice of the work slowly enough to follow and show where it fits the field.
limit: No slide count or timing given.

citation: Penn State. How to Create an Assertion-Evidence Presentation. Instruction set. Undated.
supports: Suggests 28 pt headlines, 18 to 24 pt body text, and practice of about five times the talk length, as a rule of thumb.
limit: Sizes and the practice rule carry no evidence.

citation: Garner JK, Alley M, Gaudelli AF, Zappe SE. Common use of PowerPoint versus the assertion-evidence structure: a cognitive psychology perspective. Tech Commun. 2009;56(4):331-345.
supports: Content analysis of about 2,000 slides: phrase headlines and bullets were the common pattern, including among PhD students presenting in English as an additional language.
limit: Descriptive, no audience outcome. Not a random sample.

citation: Garner JK, Alley MP. How the design of presentation slides affects audience comprehension: a case for the assertion-evidence approach. Int J Eng Educ. 2013;29(6):1564-1579.
supports: Randomised experiment with 110 engineering undergraduates: the assertion-evidence version of a recorded talk gave better comprehension and recall, with less reported effort.
limit: A bundle of changes on one recorded talk, one university. An author is the method's advocate.

citation: Farkas DK. A brief assessment of Michael Alley's ideas regarding the design of PowerPoint slides. Informal document, University of Washington; 2010.
supports: Critique: comparing against poorly designed slides is a weak test, and competent bullets do no harm.
limit: Informal memo, not peer reviewed. Predates the 2013 experiment.

citation: Mayer RE, Moreno R. Nine ways to reduce cognitive load in multimedia learning. Educ Psychol. 2003;38(1):43-52.
supports: Removing extraneous material helped learning. Identical on-screen text harmed learning alongside animation, but with no animation, narration plus text did better than narration alone.
limit: Short computer lessons with students, not live talks.

citation: Kosslyn SM, Kievit RA, Russell AG, Shephard JM. PowerPoint presentation flaws and failures: a psychological analysis. Front Psychol. 2012;3:230.
supports: Audiences most often reported too much material before the next slide, and observers were poor at spotting flaws.
limit: Prevalence and annoyance, not learning. Convenience samples.

citation: Rougier NP, Droettboom M, Bourne PE. Ten simple rules for better figures. PLoS Comput Biol. 2014;10(9):e1003833.
supports: Decide the message first, adapt figures for the medium, do not trust defaults, avoid distortion and decoration.
limit: Editorial advice.

citation: Heer J, Bostock M. Crowdsourcing graphical perception: using Mechanical Turk to assess visualization design. Proc CHI 2010:203-212.
supports: Replicated classic perception results: judgements of position beat length, and length beat angle and area.
limit: Proportion judgements online with crowd workers, not projected slides.

citation: Cleveland WS, McGill R. Graphical perception: theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. J Am Stat Assoc. 1984;79(387):531-554.
supports: Original work on perceptual ordering, cited as the study Heer and Bostock replicated.
limit: Full text not opened. We rest teaching claims on Heer and Bostock.

citation: Weissgerber TL, Milic NM, Winham SJ, Garovic VD. Beyond bar and line graphs: time for a new data presentation paradigm. PLoS Biol. 2015;13(4):e1002128.
supports: Different datasets can give the same bar chart, so show individual points for small continuous datasets.
limit: One field. Applies to continuous data, not to counts or proportions.

citation: Correll M, Bertini E, Franconeri S. Truncating the y-axis: threat or menace? Proc CHI 2020:1-12.
supports: Truncated axes made changes look more severe, even when readers could read values, but the authors reject a blanket start-at-zero rule.
limit: Small online samples, context-free charts.

citation: Pandey AV, Rall K, Satterthwaite ML, Nov O, Bertini E. How deceptive are deceptive visualizations? An empirical analysis of common distortion techniques. Proc CHI 2015:1469-1478.
supports: In online experiments truncated bars made a difference seem larger, and an inverted axis reversed the message for most readers.
limit: Paid online participants and simple charts.

citation: Wilke CO. Fundamentals of Data Visualization. O'Reilly Media; 2019. Online edition.
supports: Bars must start at zero, dot plots need not. Use few categorical colours, label directly, test in a colour-vision simulator. Gives the Okabe and Ito hex values.
limit: One expert's judgement. Licence bars derivatives, so nothing is reproduced here.

citation: Crameri F, Shephard GE, Heron PJ. The misuse of colour in science communication. Nat Commun. 2020;11:5444.
supports: Rainbow colour maps can distort data. Perceptually ordered maps stay readable in greyscale.
limit: Concerns continuous colour maps. Audience effects inferred.

citation: Okabe M, Ito K. Color Universal Design (CUD): how to make figures and presentations that are friendly to colorblind people. Web page; 2002, modified 2008.
supports: Add shape, position, line type or direct labels so that information survives without colour. Do not point things out by colour name alone.
limit: Expert guidance. Prevalence figures vary by population.

citation: World Wide Web Consortium. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum). W3C Recommendation; 2024. With Understanding SC 1.4.3.
supports: Level AA asks for 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text.
limit: Written for web content. The 18 pt threshold defines large text for contrast and is not a font minimum.

citation: World Wide Web Consortium. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color. W3C Recommendation; 2024.
supports: Colour must not be the only way of conveying information.
limit: Web scope. See WCAG2ICT for documents.

citation: W3C Accessibility Guidelines Working Group. Guidance on Applying WCAG 2 to Non-Web Information and Communications Technologies. W3C Group Note; 2025.
supports: Lists presentations among non-web documents and treats the contrast criterion as applicable to documents.
limit: Informative note, so slides are not bound to comply.

citation: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative. Making Events Accessible. Updated 2022.
supports: Make text readable from the back of the room, limit text, speak clearly, cover what is on the slide, repeat questions.
limit: Consensus checklist, not evidence of effect.

citation: Microsoft Support. Make your PowerPoint presentations accessible to people with disabilities. Web page.
supports: Give every slide a unique title, check reading order, write alt text, and use 18 pt or larger.
limit: Vendor documentation that changes with versions.

citation: von Zansen M, Craven J, adapted from World Blind Union guidelines. How to make visual presentations accessible to audience members with print impairments. University of Saskatchewan.
supports: Suggests no less than 32 pt, and short lines, for audiences with print impairments.
limit: Secondary summary, with no evidence given for its numbers.

citation: Legge GE, Bigelow CA. Does print size matter for reading? A review of findings from vision science and typography. J Vis. 2011;11(5):8.
supports: Legibility depends on angular size at the eye, so a point size means little without screen size and distance.
limit: Concerns running text at reading distance, not slides.

citation: Munro MJ, Derwing TM. Foreign accent, comprehensibility, and intelligibility in the speech of second language learners. Lang Learn. 1995;45(1):73-97.
supports: A strong accent did not necessarily reduce how well speech was understood.
limit: Abstract only. Small study, one first-language group, short utterances.

citation: Derwing TM, Munro MJ. Putting accent in its place: rethinking obstacles to communication. Lang Teach. 2009;42(4):476-490.
supports: Pronunciation work has moved from native-like speech towards easy intelligibility.
limit: Abstract only. Narrative plenary paper.

citation: Ebrahimi OV, Pallesen S, Kenter RMF, Nordgreen T. Psychological interventions for the fear of public speaking: a meta-analysis. Front Psychol. 2019;10:488.
supports: Structured psychological interventions reduced fear of public speaking in 30 randomised trials.
limit: Measures fear, not talk quality. A short workshop is not such an intervention.

citation: Streeter J, Miller FJ. Any questions? A concise guide to navigating the Q&A session after a presentation. EMBO Rep. 2011;12(3):202-205.
supports: Rehearse questions, repeat them, say when you do not know, and offer to follow up. Do not argue with hostile questions.
limit: Experience-based advice for bioscience talks.

citation: Dunphy J. Guidelines for Successful Q & A Sessions. MIT 21G.232/233 Advanced Speaking and Critical Listening Skills (ELS). MIT OpenCourseWare; 2007.
supports: A four-step answer for speakers of English as an additional language: acknowledge, check, answer, check again.
limit: One course handout. Not tested.

citation: University of Waterloo, Electrical and Computer Engineering. Technical Presentation Proficiency Examination guidelines: Questions. Undated web page.
supports: Do not bluff. Admitting you do not know costs less credibility than a wrong answer.
limit: Local exam guidance. Some of its style advice differs from other sources.

citation: Northern Illinois University. Handling Questions and Answers. Effective Presentation Skills Tutorial. Undated.
supports: Separate valid criticism from attack and answer the valid part.
limit: General, not specific to science.

citation: Hattie J, Timperley H. The power of feedback. Rev Educ Res. 2007;77(1):81-112.
supports: Feedback about the task and how to improve it helps most. Feedback aimed at the person rarely helps.
limit: Mostly school evidence, so applying it to adults is an extrapolation.

citation: Double KS, McGrane JA, Hopfenbeck TN. The impact of peer assessment on academic performance: a meta-analysis of control group studies. Educ Psychol Rev. 2020;32:481-509.
supports: Peer assessment improved academic performance on average, with a smaller estimate in tertiary students.
limit: High heterogeneity. Not specific to oral presentation or to professionals.

citation: Imperial College London. Procedure for Conducting Viva Voce Examinations for Research Degrees Programmes. Version 1.0; June 2026.
supports: A private oral examination with no prescribed length or format, where the student explains and defends the thesis.
limit: One UK university.

citation: University of Minnesota, Electrical and Computer Engineering. Graduate Handbook: PhD Final Exam. Web page.
supports: A public presentation followed by a closed session with the committee.
limit: One department.

citation: UCLA Neuroscience Interdepartmental Program. Defense. Web page.
supports: A public talk of 45 to 60 minutes accessible to a general audience, open questions, then a closed session.
limit: One programme.

citation: Halmstad University. A guide to the procedure for the public defence of a doctoral thesis. Web page.
supports: A public defence with an external opponent, usually lasting two to three hours, and a board deciding in private.
limit: One university. Practice varies by faculty.

citation: Kan E, Balivada P, Perez C, Goel V. Defense Season Wrapped: What Makes a Thesis Defense Great? MIT Biological Engineering Communication Lab; February 2026.
supports: Build background for the whole room, organise for clarity rather than chronology, and close with significance, limits and next steps.
limit: Observations of defences of about 45 minutes. Does not apply to a viva.

citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC Clear Communication Index: User Guide. August 2019, with Full Index Score Sheet.
supports: Before scoring a public material, state its audience, objective and main message. The index scores applicable items as a percentage, with 90 as CDC's passing level.
limit: Built for public health materials, not papers. A high score does not show readers understood.

citation: Gopen GD, Swan JA. The science of scientific writing. American Scientist. 1990;78(6):550-558.
supports: Readers look to the start of a sentence for context and to the end for emphasis. Keep the verb close to its subject.
limit: An argued essay with no reader data. The authors say these are not rules.

citation: Plain Language Action and Information Network. Federal Plain Language Guidelines. March 2011, revised May 2011. Reposted by the Center for Plain Language.
supports: Start with the audience, use active voice and real verbs where suitable, and test with readers.
limit: Written for US government documents. The former plainlanguage.gov link now redirects.

citation: Digital.gov. Plain language guide series. Undated web guide.
supports: Plain language matches words and detail to what readers know. It does not mean oversimplifying.
limit: Shorter successor guide. Pages show no date.

citation: MIT Communication Lab. Journal Article Abstract. Broad Institute CommKit. Undated web page.
supports: Write the abstract last, and let the reader decide whether the paper is worth reading.
limit: Tailored to basic biomedical papers. Journal rules take precedence.

citation: The Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Abstracts. Undated handout.
supports: Informative abstracts stand in for the work and give main results and conclusions.
limit: Written for all disciplines. CC BY-NC-ND, so linked and not adapted.

citation: University of Manchester. Academic Phrasebank: Being cautious. Undated web page.
supports: Writers soften claims where uncertainty remains, most often when explaining findings.
limit: A phrase bank. Does not say how strong a claim should be.

citation: Altman DG, Bland JM. Statistics notes: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ. 1995;311(7003):485.
supports: A non-significant result usually shows a lack of evidence of a difference, not evidence of no difference.
limit: Short methods note with selected examples.

citation: Wasserstein RL, Lazar NA. The ASA's statement on p-values: context, process, and purpose. Am Stat. 2016;70(2):129-133.
supports: P-values do not measure effect size or importance, and decisions should not rest on a threshold alone.
limit: Principles, not reporting rules. Does not ban p-values.

citation: Greenland S, Senn SJ, Rothman KJ, Carlin JB, Poole C, Goodman SN, Altman DG. Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations. Eur J Epidemiol. 2016;31:337-350.
supports: P above 0.05 does not show no effect. Interval width indicates precision.
limit: Conceptual guide. Dense for beginners.

citation: Lang TA, Altman DG. Basic statistical reporting for articles published in biomedical journals: the SAMPL Guidelines. Int J Nurs Stud. 2015;52(1):5-9.
supports: Give numerators and denominators for percentages, and effect estimates with precision, usually a 95% CI.
limit: Not built by formal consensus. Journal style can override details.

citation: Sumner P, Vivian-Griffiths S, Boivin J, et al. The association between exaggeration in health related science news and academic press releases: retrospective observational study. BMJ. 2014;349:g7015.
supports: About a third of 462 university press releases made stronger causal claims than the journal article, and exaggeration in news was associated with exaggeration in releases.
limit: Correlational. One country and year. A correction exists (BMJ 2014;349:g7666), and its detail was not seen, so check it before quoting further figures.

citation: Haber N, Smith ER, Moscoe E, et al. Causal language and strength of inference in academic and media articles shared in social media (CLAIMS): a systematic review. PLoS One. 2018;13(5):e0196346.
supports: A third of the academic papers reviewed used language too strong for their inference.
limit: Most-shared stories only, so not representative of research at large.

citation: Haber NA, Wieten SE, Rohrer JM, et al. Causal and associational language in observational health research: a systematic evaluation. Am J Epidemiol. 2022;191(12):2084-2097.
supports: Many reviewers read some causal meaning into the word association, and recommendations often imply more causality than the linking sentence.
limit: High-profile journals only.

citation: Hernan MA. The C-word: scientific euphemisms do not improve causal inference from observational data. Am J Public Health. 2018;108(5):616-619.
supports: State a causal aim openly rather than hiding it behind associational wording.
limit: Commentary. Journals may still ask authors to avoid causal terms.

citation: van der Bles AM, van der Linden S, Freeman ALJ, et al. Communicating uncertainty about facts, numbers and science. R Soc Open Sci. 2019;6(5):181870.
supports: Separates uncertainty about a number from uncertainty about the quality of the evidence behind it.
limit: Narrative review.

citation: van der Bles AM, van der Linden S, Freeman ALJ, Spiegelhalter DJ. The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2020;117(14):7672-7683.
supports: In five experiments, numeric ranges cost little trust, and verbal uncertainty cost more.
limit: UK public and non-health topics.

citation: Santesso N, Glenton C, Dahm P, et al. GRADE guidelines 26: informative statements to communicate the findings of systematic reviews of interventions. J Clin Epidemiol. 2020;119:126-135.
supports: Convey both effect size and certainty. Wording steps down from 'results in' to 'likely' to 'may', and vague phrases such as 'limited evidence' should be replaced.
limit: Built for systematic reviews, and needs a certainty rating.

citation: Gigerenzer G, Gaissmaier W, Kurz-Milcke E, Schwartz LM, Woloshin S. Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychol Sci Public Interest. 2007;8(2):53-96.
supports: Recommends absolute risks and frequency statements over relative risks and single-event probabilities.
limit: Narrative review with a clear point of view.

citation: Akl EA, Oxman AD, Herrin J, et al. Using alternative statistical formats for presenting risks and risk reductions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2011;(3):CD006776.
supports: Relative reductions looked larger and persuaded more than absolute ones, with no difference in understanding. So do not give the relative figure alone.
limit: Search to 2007. Mostly hypothetical scenarios.

citation: Vandenbroucke JP, von Elm E, Altman DG, et al. Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE): explanation and elaboration. PLoS Med. 2007;4(10):e297.
supports: Abstracts should give key results as numbers with effect estimates and uncertainty. Adjustment does not by itself establish causation.
limit: A reporting guide, not a quality score. Observational studies only.

citation: Hopewell S, Clarke M, Moher D, et al. CONSORT for reporting randomized controlled trials in journal and conference abstracts: explanation and elaboration. PLoS Med. 2008;5(1):e20.
supports: Readers often judge a trial from its abstract alone, so report results for each group with effect size and precision.
limit: Trials only. Not yet aligned with CONSORT 2025.

citation: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors. Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals. Updated January 2026.
supports: Sets four authorship criteria, requires permission for acknowledgement, protects patient identity, and says humans remain responsible for AI-assisted work, which must be disclosed.
limit: Applies to journals that follow it.

citation: COPE Council. COPE position: Authorship and AI tools. Committee on Publication Ethics; reviewed February 2023.
supports: AI tools cannot be authors. Authors are responsible for all content and must disclose use.
limit: Differs from ICMJE on where to disclose, so follow the target journal.

citation: US Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights. Guidance Regarding Methods for De-identification of Protected Health Information in Accordance with the HIPAA Privacy Rule.
supports: Initials and parts of identifiers still count as identifiers, and de-identification does not bring risk to zero.
limit: US law for covered entities. Gives no small-cell rule.

citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Recital 26.
supports: Pseudonymised data remain personal data. Identifiability depends on means reasonably likely to be used.
limit: A recital aids interpretation. Read through an unofficial copy.

citation: Public Health Scotland. Statistical disclosure control protocol. Version 2.2; June 2024.
supports: Small cells, and differences between tables, can identify people. Rates can reveal small counts, and small numbers can expose a clinician.
limit: One agency's protocol. Thresholds differ, so find your institution's rule.

citation: Walters WH, Wilder EI. Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Sci Rep. 2023;13:14045.
supports: Many citations from two 2023 models pointed to works that do not exist, so a plausible citation is not a verified one.
limit: A snapshot of old models. Shows a failure mode, not a current rate.

citation: Peters U, Chin-Yee B. Generalization bias in large language model summarization of scientific research. R Soc Open Sci. 2025;12(4):241776.
supports: Most models tested broadened claims when summarising science, and asking for accuracy did not help.
limit: Version-specific results that will age.
